questions.prompt: After a credible next objective is chosen, what question does Chapter 9 add?
choices: Whether a weak indispensable link is capping the system
Whether every part should be improved equally
Whether average strength is now enough

questions.prompt: What best defines a chain-link system in this chapter?
choices: A system improved by average strength alone
A system capped by its weakest indispensable link
A system where every weak part matters equally
questions.explanation: Chain-link systems are limited by the weakest necessary link rather than by average strength.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter reject compensation logic?
choices: Because strong links elsewhere cannot offset a failed critical link
Because all parts are always equally important
Because broad improvement is never useful
questions.explanation: In a chain-link system, one indispensable weak link can still cap the whole result.

choices: The indispensable weak link that caps the whole result
The strongest area in the system
The average performance across all parts

It can leave the real bottleneck untouched
It creates too much local success

A celebration of the stronger parts

questions.prompt: What is the strongest sign that a system is chain-link limited?
choices: One indispensable weak step keeps capping the whole result
Many parts are slightly below average
The team feels pressure to improve everything
questions.explanation: A chain-link system is signaled by one weak necessary link setting the whole ceiling.

choices: Because strong parts never matter
Because a broken indispensable link can still govern the result
Because averages are always irrelevant
questions.explanation: The weak indispensable link can dominate the result even when other parts are strong.

choices: Turning toward design and structural constraint logic
Returning to broad average-strength improvement
Ignoring system structure and focusing on effort
